practice.taskOpening: Initialize TensorFlow.js, wait for it to be ready, and return an object containing the active backend name and TF.js version, shaped `{ backend, version }`. practice.title: Compute FFT and Find Dominant Frequency
practice.taskOpening: Write a function that takes a signal array and a sample rate, computes the FFT with tf.spectral.rfft(), and returns the dominant frequency in hertz: the frequency of the highest-magnitude bin, with the DC component at bin 0 excluded. A spectrum only has bin centers to offer, so the answer is the center of the winning bin. For an isolated off-bin tone, the winning bin often lies near the tone. Phase, leakage, neighboring components and boundary bins can change the winner; nearest-bin rounding is not the algorithm. Use the computed magnitudes. Assume finite input with at least two samples and a positive sample rate. Break equal-magnitude ties by keeping the lowest eligible bin.

practice.title: Build a Spectrogram
practice.taskOpening: Implement `stft(signal, windowSize, hopSize)`, one FFT per window position stacked in time. Window i starts at sample i * hopSize, and a window counts only when it fits inside the signal whole, so the row count comes out of all three arguments. Each row is the magnitude spectrum of that window's own samples, left in bin order, and rfft returns floor(windowSize / 2) + 1 of those magnitudes, which is 33 for a 64-sample window. Return the rows in time order as a 2D array with one row per window position and one column per frequency bin. Cut each window straight out of the signal with no taper, so a row is the plain magnitude spectrum of the raw slice: tf.signal.stft applies a Hann window by default, and its rows will not match. Assume integer windowSize >= 2 and hopSize >= 1. Return an empty array when no complete window fits.

First the peak amplitude: the largest absolute sample value in the capture. Then the zero-crossing count: how many times consecutive samples land on opposite sides of zero. Then one FFT magnitude per fixed bin whose center falls inside the band from loHz to hiHz, endpoints included. Bin width is sampleRate divided by the number of samples, so 64 samples at 256 Hz gives 4 Hz bins and the 50 to 82 Hz band is bins 13 through 20. Leave the magnitudes in bin order. Sorting them by size would make the third feature mean a different frequency in every row. Report each magnitude at the height the transform gives it, unscaled: the normalization the lesson describes is measured across a whole training set and applied after extraction, not inside this function.
Assume finite, nonempty captures, a positive sample rate and 0 <= loHz <= hiHz <= sampleRate / 2.
Here a crossing means strictly opposite signs on adjacent samples: one positive and one negative. A pair containing an exact zero contributes nothing. Other conventions exist; this exercise uses that one consistently.

practice.title: Detect Anomalies with Z-Score
practice.taskOpening: Write `isAnomaly(value, mean, std)` that returns true when the reading sits more than 3 standard deviations from the mean, in either direction. practice.title: Temporal Attention Over a Window
practice.taskOpening:
Build `temporalAttention(sequence, scorerWeights)`. `sequence` is a [T, d] tensor of readings; `scorerWeights` is a [d + 1, 1] linear scorer whose last row weights position. Concatenate a position column onto the readings, evenly spaced from 0 at the first step to 1 at the last. Score every step with one matMul, then softmax those scores into `weights`, a [T] tensor holding one weight per step. Pool the ORIGINAL readings under those weights into a [d] `summary`, and return `{ summary, weights }` with both still tensors. Skip the position column and the scorer's shape will not line up.
Remove only the batch axis. A value width of one must still return shape [1], not a scalar. The sequence is non-empty; for a single time step its position is 0. Free intermediates with tf.tidy, preserving caller-owned inputs and both returned tensors.

practice.title: Incident: Cache Served a Verdict From the Old Model
practice.taskOpening: PAGER: after this morning's model deploy, the dashboard showed a classification the new model disagrees with. It came from the cache. Build `auditCache(entries, currentVersion, now, ttlSeconds)`: an entry must be REFRESHED if its modelVersion differs from currentVersion (a deploy invalidates every cached verdict, no matter how fresh) OR its age (now - cachedAt, seconds) exceeds ttlSeconds. An age of exactly ttlSeconds has not exceeded it, so that entry is still served. Everything else passes this age/version policy, not a general correctness test. Assume valid timestamps no later than now and nonnegative finite TTL. The version identifies both weights and preprocessing; approximate-key collisions need separate checks. Return { serve, refresh } as arrays of keys, preserving input order.
